title: Connexions de Gauss-Manin et équations de Picard-Fuchs. Opération de Cartier : copies de tapuscrit annoté (s.d.), tiré à part (1981), notes manuscrites (s.d.).

deep.reconstruction:
Context: this page continues a functorial re-statement of the uniformization theorem. It is groundwork for attaching a canonical flat projective-line bundle to any Riemann surface, which belongs with the Gauss–Manin and Picard–Fuchs material of this folder.

(1) End of the corollary on stabilizers of homogeneous domains in a projective line P over C. Here GP(1) is Grothendieck's notation for the projective group PGL_2. In cases 1 (D = P) and 2 (D = P minus a point) the stabilizers are complex algebraic groups: PGL_2(C) and Aff(1,C). In case 3 (D a disc) the stabilizer is the group of real points GP(1)(R) of a real algebraic group GP(1)_R, which is a real form of GP(1)_C.

Grothendieck states that such real forms correspond bijectively with four kinds of data:
- (α) a descent of Aut_C P from C to R;
- (β) a real form of the complex Lie algebra Lie Aut_C P = H^0(P, T_{P/C}) ≅ H^0(P, Ω^{-1}) ≅ sl_2(C);
- (γ) a disc-type homogeneous domain D in P, up to 'polarity' (D is identified with its polar, apparently P minus the closure of D);
- (δ, marginal addition) a circle in P.

The passage from δ to γ: a real projective line P_R with P_R ⊗_R C = P has real points P_R(R), which form a circle in P(C). The complement has two connected components, both discs, exchanged by inversion in the circle, i.e. complex conjugation.

(2) Scholie. On the category (isomorphisms only) of connected, simply connected non-singular analytic curves X there is a functor X ↦ P(X), valued in complex projective lines. It comes with a functorial embedding i_X : X ↪ P(X)(C) making X a homogeneous domain. The pair (P, i) is unique up to unique isomorphism. This is a rigidified, functorial form of the Riemann mapping / uniformization theorem.

(3) Now let X be an arbitrary non-singular analytic curve. For each x, let X~(x) be the universal cover based at x. As x varies, these form a local system on the fundamental groupoid Π(X), valued in simply connected curves.
- The projections X~(x) → X form a morphism of local systems.
- Hence one gets a relative analytic space X~ → X × X over X (via pr_2), carrying integrable connections (genuine parallel transport) that the morphism respects.
- The tautological section x ↦ x~ maps to the diagonal, which proves it is analytic.
- This part works for any analytic space; in effect X~ → X × X is the fundamental groupoid seen as an analytic space with source and target maps.

For curves, applying the functor P fibrewise gives a canonical analytic P^1-bundle P_X over X. It has:
- an integrable connection;
- an analytic section σ;
- an open embedding X~ ⊂ P_X whose fibres are homogeneous domains.

The next page states this as Théorème 2. In modern terms this is the uniformizing projective structure on X: a flat PGL_2-bundle with a section (Gunning's 'indigenous bundle', the uniformizing PGL_2-oper). Its local description is the Schwarzian / uniformizing second-order linear ODE. That ODE is where Picard–Fuchs equations meet uniformization: for example, the Legendre Picard–Fuchs equation uniformizes X(2).
errors: The bijection α ↔ β ↔ γ ↔ δ is only correct for split real forms. PGL_2,C (and sl_2(C)) also has the compact real form PU(2) ≅ SO(3), with Lie algebra su(2). It corresponds to the real form of P without real points (the antipodal involution, a conic with no real points), and to no circle or disc. As written, α) and β) must be restricted to forms whose real points are non-compact, equivalently descents of P with real points.

In γ), 'up to polarity' should be read as identifying the two complementary discs of a circle; the parenthetical 'la polaire de D est P−D̄' is only half legible. With this identification the γ–δ correspondence is a bijection.
The Scholie's functor must be on the groupoid (isomorphisms only) of simply connected curves, as the previous page specifies. Non-invertible holomorphic maps, e.g. disc → C, do not extend to P^1.

ideas.what: Real forms of PGL_2 / sl_2 correspond to circles in P^1 (antiholomorphic reflections) and to pairs of complementary discs; the stabilizer of a disc is the real points of a real form
ideas.modern_name: Real forms of PGL_2 and anti-holomorphic involutions of CP^1 (Cartan classification)

ideas.what: Functorial uniformization: a functor P from simply connected Riemann surfaces to projective lines with a natural embedding as homogeneous domain, unique up to unique isomorphism
ideas.modern_name: Uniformization theorem (Koebe–Poincaré) in rigidified functorial form

ideas.what: Universal covers at all base points form a local system over Π(X); this yields an analytic space X~ → X×X with integrable connection and canonical section over the diagonal
ideas.modern_name: Fundamental (monodromy) groupoid as an analytic/Lie groupoid; universal cover as a flat relative space

ideas.what: Canonical flat P^1-bundle P_X with section and embedded X~ attached to any Riemann surface
ideas.modern_name: Uniformizing projective structure / indigenous bundle / uniformizing PGL_2-oper
ideas.usually_credited_to: Gunning (1966–67, 'Lectures on Riemann surfaces', indigenous bundles); later Beilinson–Drinfeld (opers), Mochizuki (p-adic Teichmüller theory)

missed.claim: Grothendieck places the canonical uniformizing flat P^1-bundle (an indigenous bundle) in the same folder as Gauss–Manin connections, Picard–Fuchs equations and the Cartier operation. This suggests treating the uniformizing connection algebraically alongside Gauss–Manin connections, and implicitly studying its p-curvature or Cartier behaviour. That is exactly the later programme of Mochizuki (p-adic Teichmüller theory, dormant and ordinary indigenous bundles) and of the theory of opers in characteristic p. This page itself only builds the analytic object, so the link is suggestive rather than explicit.
missed.quote: d'où un fibré projectif canonique sur X, noté P_X, avec une connexion intégrable
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Historically it would document that Grothendieck independently formulated the uniformizing indigenous bundle in a Gauss–Manin / Cartier context, possibly before Mochizuki's work. Mathematically the object is already well known (Gunning 1967).

deep.surprise_reason: The content is classical: uniformization, real forms of PGL_2, and projective structures as flat P^1-bundles with a section (Gunning). The only notable features are Grothendieck's characteristically functorial, base-point-free construction through the fundamental groupoid, and the fact that it sits in a Gauss–Manin / Cartier-operation folder.
transcription_corrections: 'GP(1)' is Grothendieck's notation for the projective group PGL_2 (automorphisms of P^1), not a typo.
Marginal insertion δ) is barely legible; it reads roughly 'δ) choix d'un ... (= cercle) dans P'. 'géodésique' is uncertain.
The polarity parenthesis likely reads '(la polaire de D est P − D̄)', i.e. the complement of the closure of D.
In the Scholie, 'homomorphisme fonctoriel' may be 'monomorphisme' or 'immersion fonctorielle', given the hooked arrow X ↪ P(X)(C).
'Lie Aut_C P = H^0(P, V_{P/C})', with V the tangent sheaf, ≅ H^0(P, Ω^{-1}_{P/C}).
